To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dietary supplementation with L-carnosines in 3x-Tg-AD mice ameliorates mitochondrial dysfunction and amyloid-β pathology.
carnosine treatment of the 3x Tg-AD mice, a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, rescues the age-related and disease-associated mitochondrial dysfunction and reduces the intraneuronal Aβ burden.
carnosine is effective in reducing amyloid-beta accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a therapeutic intervention for AD, which is based on the use of carnosine, a naturally occurring compound that is able to counteract several pathogenic processes that contribute to AD.
a better understanding of carnosine effects and its potential therapeutic application in AD.
the development of a new therapeutic approach to AD, based on a combination of drugs that can target the different pathological hallmarks of the disorder.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

carnosine, as well as other antioxidants, can only be considered as a supportive treatment for AD and that the best strategy for the treatment of this disease would still be a combination of different drugs, each one targeting different aspects of the disease, as well as lifestyle changes.
carnosine, by reducing Aβ levels, may be beneficial in the treatment for AD, but it does not appear to have any direct effect on tau pathology and cognitive deficits.
the effects of carnosine on the AD pathology and on cognitive deficits in the 3×Tg-AD model are not as clear-cut as those observed on mitochondrial dysfunction and amyloid pathology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

carnosine, a natural compound with a long history in dietary supplements, is effective in reducing the intraneuronal amyloid-β load, rescuing the mitochondrial dysfunction, and improving the cognitive deficits of 3xTG-AD mice.
L-carnosin, a natural dipeptide, can improve mitochondrial function and Aβ burden in 3x Tg-AD mouse model, and can potentially be a candidate for AD therapy.
L-carnosin supplementation is able to rescue AD-related mitochondrial dysfunction, but not cognitive impairment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mitochondrial dysfunction is a critical factor in AD pathology and that carnosine may help to restore mitochondrial function in AD.
the beneficial effects of carnosine supplementation are mainly related to the prevention of mitochondrial dysfunctions and Aβ accumulation.
carnosine may have a role in the prevention of AD and in the treatment of the cognitive decline associated with this disease.
